articles.title: The Uprising Wastes a Good Class-Struggle Story
articles.author: Jeremy Gong
articles.content_excerpt: In 1381, more than a hundred thousand poor English people rose up demanding an end to serfdom. During the uprising, they killed a coterie of hated government officials, and, in turn, the fourteen-year-old King Richard II massacred thousands of them. The best-remembered figure of the English Peasants’ Revolt is one of its leaders, John Ball, whose speeches and sermons captured the spirit of what would eventually, centuries later, develop into socialism. “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?” he famously asked, meaning that in the Garden of Eden, the Bible’s first people labored only for their own sustenance, with no concepts of lords and serfs. articles.title: The Prospects for a 2028 May Day Mass Strike
articles.author: Luis Feliz Leon
articles.content_excerpt: Three years ago, the United Auto Workers (UAW), glowing with confidence after a successful strike at the Big Three and pledging ambitious new organizing drives, put out a call for a national strike on May 1, 2028. UAW President Shawn Fain called for unions to align their contracts with the Big Three to build leverage and create a crisis for the billionaire class. It was a new day in the UAW, and a wider labor renewal felt possible. May 2028 is now only a year and a half away. Are unions getting in gear for a season of strikes and labor action around then, as contracts expire in manufacturing, education, logistics, grocery, and the building trades? Some are. articles.title: American Reality Is Beyond Parody, but Satire Isn’t Dead
articles.author: Michael G. Vann
articles.content_excerpt: A specter is haunting contemporary American satire: the specter of reality. This specter poses an existential threat to comedy as social critique. How do you make jokes in this era of hyperabsurdity? Donald Trump’s two administrations sandwiched four years of Joe Biden mumbling incoherently as he stumbling around. Corporations speak in the language of therapy, and airlines charge passengers for micro-comforts while advertising travel as an expression of personal freedom. Billionaires promise to colonize Mars while American cities see their bridges collapse. Streamers make a career out of broadcasting themselves gambling, eating, fighting, shopping, hurling insults, and slowly losing their minds. Kash Patel exists. articles.title: France’s Left Faces the 2027 Election Divided
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content_excerpt: Over Christmastime 2018, Jean-Luc Mélenchon met for lunch with Raphaël Glucksmann in France’s National Assembly. Mélenchon was an MP at the time, fresh off his strong 2017 presidential run for France Insoumise. Glucksmann was a liberal essayist with a murky background advising sometimes-dubious politicians in countries like Ukraine and Georgia, producing documentaries about human rights issues while looking to get into politics himself. The conversation stayed light and nonconfrontational, and they were joined by the former Socialist Emmanuel Maurel (at that time supportive of France Insoumise), and Thomas Porcher, an economist who’d voted for Mélenchon the year before. articles.title: Debating Victor Serge
articles.author: Mitchell Abidor
articles.content_excerpt: When I began writing Victor Serge: Unruly Revolutionary , I expected to write a biography in keeping with the image common on the left of Serge as an uncompromising enemy of Stalinism who never fell into anti-communism and fought all his life for revolutionary socialism. This is what we find in the many writings of Richard Greeman, who single-handedly rescued Serge from oblivion by translating his novels and tirelessly writing about him. In fact, my biography began as a collaboration between me and Richard, one we abandoned due to differences in interpretation. Suzi Weissman presents that image as well in her biography of Serge, The Course Is Set on Hope . A fuller account of this Serge was what I thought I was going to write. articles.title: Flock Off: How Westland DSA Members Pushed Flock Cameras Out of Their City
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content_excerpt: By filling city council meetings, educating the public on mass surveillance, and cooperating with like-minded allies, DSA members in Westland shot down a Flock contract renewal. By Dave N. and Kathy E. In July 2024 the city of Westland signed up for a trial run with Flock Safety that would last until August 2026. Flock’s cameras are Automated License Plate Readers (ALPR) that mark the date, time, and location where a vehicle passes. Flock claims that its technology does not scan human faces, but its cameras are able to fingerprint cars based on minute details like rust or bumper stickers. The technology is similar to that used in facial recognition software. articles.title: Six Hail Marys: Thoughts of an ICU RN
articles.author: Red Fault -- Austin DSA
articles.content_excerpt: By Asanti M. The conversation surrounding healthcare access is more than an abstraction of cost and risk, it’s life and death, and people are dying. I know because I’ve pronounced them. I know because I’ve cleaned their lifeless bodies. The burdens of the ailing are only compounded by the general disservice of our institutional frameworks. The nebulous jargon tossed around boardrooms and between pundits materializes in the financial reality that confronts the humanity of the unfortunate and the ailing. I’ve seen eyes full of pain, the walls of life crumbling around them, forced to discuss the finances of death, because let me be clear, dying is a very expensive endeavor hear in the States, and God forbid you attempt to hold on to life! articles.title: Texas Wasn’t Always a Right-Wing Evangelical Powerhouse
articles.author: David Griscom
articles.content_excerpt: There’s a common view of religious history that holds that the further back you go, the stronger the smell of brimstone and the more conservative the beliefs. It isn’t true, and it obscures how much the human hand makes the world, including our ideas of the sacred. Joseph L. Locke’s new book One State Under God: A History of Religion in Texas is an important reminder that the conservative evangelical Christianity that dominates Texas, and through it has consolidated its influence over the country, was not a natural outgrowth of Christianity itself, but a product of historical developments. Texas today is at the forefront of the campaign to tear down the wall between church and state.
